extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent claims for compliance with 35 U.S.C. §112, second paragraph (definiteness), including treatment of functional language, terms of degree/subjective terms, Markush groups, dependent claims, and means-plus-function (§112, sixth paragraph) limitations; also includes prosecution and drafting recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination, a claim must be given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words of the claim must be given their plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification; the plain meaning is the ordinary and customary meaning to those of ordinary skill at the time of the invention. The specification is the best source for determining claim-term meaning and can serve as a glossary; the presumption of ordinary meaning may be rebutted if the applicant clearly sets forth a different definition in the specification. See MPEP § 2111 for full discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different Standard During Examination vs. Post-Issuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims under examination are construed under a different standard than issued patents: there is no presumption of validity and claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the patent record is still in development, a lower threshold of ambiguity is applied during prosecution. A claim should be rejected under §112, ¶2 if, after BRI, its metes and bounds are not clear (e.g., a person of ordinary skill would read it with more than one reasonable interpretation). Examiners should not conflate claim breadth with indefiniteness: breadth alone is not indefiniteness if the scope is clearly defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine Invocation of 35 U.S.C. §112, Sixth Paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should determine whether each claim limitation invokes §112, ¶6 (means-plus-function or step-plus-function) or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a limitation invokes §112, ¶6, it must be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof. See PART 1, section III.C for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional Language — Scope and Definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: For functional language (defining an item by what it does rather than by physical characteristics), consider whether the claim: (1) gives a clear-cut indication of the scope covered; (2) sets forth well-defined boundaries rather than only stating a problem to be solved or result to be obtained; and (3) would enable one of ordinary skill to know from the claim terms what structure or steps are encompassed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional language is not intrinsically improper, but unlimited functional claiming that lacks recited structure/material/steps may be indefinite or fail §112, ¶1 written description/enablement. Examples of problematic functional limitations include claims that merely describe a problem or an outcome. Examiner determinations are context-dependent (specification disclosure and knowledge of one skilled in the art are key).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for Ambiguous Functional Claiming
rubrics_metrics.description: To resolve possible ambiguities in functional claiming, applicants may (1) recite a quantitative metric rather than a qualitative functional feature; (2) show that the specification provides a formula for calculating a property along with examples that meet and do not meet the limitation; (3) show the specification provides general guidelines and examples sufficient to teach one of ordinary skill when the limitation is satisfied; or (4) amend the claims to recite the particular structure that performs the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These actions can be used in prosecution to rebut indefiniteness rejections and to clarify claim metes and bounds on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms of Degree — Definiteness Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: For terms of degree (e.g., 'substantially free of'), examiners should consider whether the specification provides some standard for measuring the recited degree or whether one of ordinary skill in the art could ascertain the scope (for example, by a standard recognized in the art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim reciting a term of degree should not be held indefinite if the specification provides examples or teachings that can be used to measure the degree even without precise numerical measurement (e.g., a drawing figure providing a standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective Terms — Need for Objective Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: For subjective terms (e.g., 'aesthetically pleasing'), examiners should consider whether the specification provides some objective standard for measuring the scope of the claim; if the claim requires unrestricted subjective judgment, it may be rejected as indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To overcome indefiniteness for terms of degree or subjective terms, an applicant may provide evidence (e.g., a 37 CFR §1.132 declaration) that one of ordinary skill can ascertain the meaning from the specification, or amend the claim to remove such terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush Group Definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush claim (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of...') may be rejected under §112, ¶2 if one of ordinary skill cannot determine the metes and bounds of the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indefiniteness can arise if the examiner cannot envision all members of the Markush group or if the species do not share a single structural similarity or a common use (not functionally equivalent). To overcome such a rejection, an applicant may provide evidence that the members share a single structural similarity or common use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent Claims — §112, Fourth Paragraph Compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: When examining a dependent claim, Examiners should determine whether the claim complies with §112, ¶4: it must contain a reference to a previous claim in the same application, further limit the claimed subject matter, and include all the limitations of the previous claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these requirements are not met, the Examiner should reject the claim under §112, ¶4. To overcome the rejection, amend the claim to properly reference the previous claim, further limit the subject matter, or include all limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-Plus-Function Claim Invocation Criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is presumed to invoke §112, ¶6 if it recites 'means for' or 'step for' and includes functional language; if it does not use these phrases, there is a strong rebuttable presumption that §112, ¶6 does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consider that a non-structural term (e.g., 'mechanism') associated with functional language may invoke §112, ¶6 unless (1) it is preceded by a structural modifier, defined in the specification or known in the art as a particular structure, or (2) it is modified by sufficient structure or material for achieving the recited function. The guidelines set three criteria to apply §112, ¶6: (1) use of 'means for'/'step for' or a non-structural term without a structural modifier; (2) the term is modified by functional language; and (3) the term is not modified by sufficient structure/material/acts for achieving the function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclear Invocation — Reject as Indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is unclear whether a claim invokes §112, ¶6, Examiners should reject the claim under §112, ¶2 as being indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a rejection requires the applicant to respond by explaining why the language is definite or by amending the claim; rejections must clearly identify the indefinite language and thoroughly explain the reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: §112, Sixth Paragraph — Written Description Link Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure that a §112, ¶6 limitation complies with §112, ¶2, the written description must clearly link or associate the corresponding structure, material, or acts to the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must disclose the corresponding structure/material/acts; for computer-implemented means-plus-function limitations, the specification must disclose an algorithm (e.g., mathematical formula, flow chart, or textual description) for performing the function. Merely stating that a function is performed by a computer or processor without disclosing an algorithm is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Practice — Err on Side of Rejection to Clarify Record
rubrics_metrics.description: The guidelines encourage Examiners to be more critical in evaluating claims for indefiniteness and to err on the side of making rejections because such a rejection requires the applicant to explain or amend, thereby clarifying claim boundaries prior to issuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect a short-term increase in §112, ¶2 rejections. Rejections must clearly identify the language causing indefiniteness and thoroughly explain the reasoning. Examiners should avoid piecemeal examination and reject each claim on all valid grounds as appropriate (see MPEP references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting and Prosecution Recommendations for Applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended applicant actions during drafting and prosecution to avoid or overcome indefiniteness rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations: (1) provide guidance in the specification for terms of degree or subjective terms; (2) decide whether to invoke §112, ¶6 and ensure claim language matches intent and the specification discloses corresponding structure/material/acts; (3) ensure algorithms are adequately disclosed for computer-implemented means-plus-function limitations; (4) ensure Markush limitations and dependent claims comply with guideline requirements; (5) consider personal interviews with Examiners to resolve §112, ¶2 rejections; (6) consider filing Rule 132 Declarations to rebut rejections (e.g., to show one of ordinary skill could determine metes and bounds, provide examples in/out of scope); and (7) carefully review Examiner claim constructions for accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing a Clear Record and Compact Prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: When resolving indefinite claim language, actions should focus on establishing a clear record, providing sufficient explanation in Office Actions, and practicing 'compact prosecution'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office Actions should identify problematic language and explain reasoning; compact prosecution aims to resolve issues efficiently and minimize unnecessary statements that could create estoppel. See PART 1 Step 3 and MPEP references for procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Evidence and Declarations to Rebut Indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may use evidence (e.g., 37 CFR §1.132 Declarations) to show that the meaning of claim language can be ascertained by one of ordinary skill in the art when reading the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence can include examples of items within and outside the claimed scope, demonstrations that the specification provides measurement standards/formulae, or other factual showing to rebut Examiner assertions of indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification as Primary Source of Claim Meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should be used as the primary source for interpreting claim terms and for providing standards or definitions to clarify terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the specification sets a clear path to claim language (e.g., defining terms, providing examples or formulas), the scope of claims is more easily determined and public notice is best served. Applicants may expressly define terms in the specification to rebut ordinary meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional Claiming Anti-Patterns and Examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples where functional or qualitative language has been held indefinite or problematic (illustrative anti-patterns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative problematic phrases include: 'fragile gel' defined functionally without clear degree, phrases reciting outcomes such as 'of such size and contour as to prevent substantial sagging or offsetting during a normal or commercially useful life', and qualitative mixtures characterized by buyer-desired standards like 'commercially uniform'. These examples show that terms describing only outcomes or subjective commercial preferences can create indefiniteness or failure to adequately define structural characteristics.
